title: Construction Brand Landscape Research
summary: Research on construction industry branding to inform AOM's vertical positioning.
content:
Construction Brand Landscape -- Steffen Research

Practice mode research. Last updated: 2026-03-08 Purpose: Know the vertical so when Patrik drops reference images, we already understand what's out there.

The Problem With Most Construction Brands

The construction industry has a massive branding gap. Companies doing $5M-$50M+ in revenue often look like they were branded by a nephew with Canva. The bar is low, which means any company that invests in real visual identity immediately separates itself.

The Generic Starter Pack (What 80% of Construction Companies Look Like)

  • Colors: Blue and orange. Every time. Sometimes navy + safety orange. Sometimes royal blue + construction yellow. It's a sea of sameness.
  • Typography: Arial, Arial Black, or whatever sans-serif came with Word. Heavy, blocky, no personality.
  • Logos: Hard hat icon. Crane silhouette. House outline. Wrench + hammer crossed. Clip art energy.
  • Photography: Stock photos of people in hard hats shaking hands. Generic aerial drone shots. Zero personality.
  • Websites: Template builders with stock imagery, bullet-point service lists, and a "Request a Quote" button that feels like it leads nowhere.
  • Social media: Inconsistent posting, no visual system, random job site photos with no composition or editing.

Why This Matters for AOM

AOM's target is 15 construction companies on social media retainers at $3k/month. The pitch writes itself when you can show a prospect what they look like now vs what they could look like. The visual gap is the sales tool.

What Standout Construction Brands Do Differently

1. They Pick a Lane and Own It

The best construction brands don't try to appeal to everyone. They choose a visual identity that reflects their actual market position:

  • High-end residential builders look editorial, almost architectural
  • Commercial contractors look corporate and polished
  • Specialty trades look bold and industrial

2. They Invest in Real Photography

The single biggest differentiator. Companies like NS Builders and Killowen Construction built massive followings (231K and 399K on Instagram, respectively) primarily through exceptional photography of their work. No stock. No clip art. Real projects, shot with intention.

3. Color Palette Has Range, Not Just a Logo Color

Standout brands have:

  • A primary brand color (not blue + orange)
  • Supporting neutrals that actually work on screens
  • An accent color for CTAs and highlights
  • Dark/light mode flexibility

4. Typography Does Heavy Lifting

Not just "a font" but a system:

  • Headlines that convey weight and confidence
  • Body type that's actually readable
  • A display or accent typeface for personality moments

5. Consistency Across Every Touchpoint

Same visual language on the truck wrap, the website, the Instagram grid, the proposal PDF, and the job site signage. This is where most construction companies completely fall apart.

Brands Worth Studying

Tier 1: The Standard (National/Large Companies With Serious Brand Investment)

Brasfield & Gorrie

  • Rebranded by Matchstic (top-tier brand agency)
  • Tagline: "Going beyond the build"
  • The redesigned ampersand in their name became a graphic element used throughout the brand
  • Modern, digitally-focused palette built on their classic blue
  • Shows how a legacy company (est. 1964) can modernize without losing trust

Skanska

  • Clean wordmark, all-uppercase, custom sans-serif with slight curves
  • "Skanska blue" is distinctive and owned. Not generic navy. Not royal blue. Their blue.
  • Simple, confident. The brand says "we don't need to prove anything."

Turner Construction

  • Heavy sans-serif wordmark (modified Helvetica Black)
  • Deep blue (#00205B range). Professional, institutional.
  • The brand works because it's unapologetically corporate. No warmth needed at their scale.

Kiewit

  • Yellow and black. Bold, industrial, immediately recognizable on job sites.
  • The color choice is strategic: you see a Kiewit truck and know it from 200 feet away.
  • Proof that standing out sometimes means ignoring what everyone else does with blue.

Tier 2: Standout Builders (Smaller Companies With Premium Visual Identity)

NS Builders (@nsbuilders) -- Boston, MA

  • 231K Instagram followers
  • High-end custom homes
  • Clean, minimal visual identity
  • The photography IS the brand. Every image is composed, lit, edited with intention.
  • Dark, moody tones mixed with bright architectural shots

Killowen Construction (@killowenconstruction) -- Orem, UT

  • 399K Instagram followers with only 1,293 posts (high curation, high engagement)
  • Selective posting strategy: fewer posts, each one hits
  • The feed itself is a portfolio. Every image could be in a magazine.

construction2style (@construction2style) -- Elk River, MN

  • Husband-wife team, 83K followers
  • "Moody, eclectic, traditional, rooted" as their stated style
  • Content-first approach: education, behind-the-scenes, personality
  • Turned their brand into a media company (courses, workshops, content partnerships)

Tier 3: Award-Winning Web Presence

Vitruvius Built

  • Won 2025 Best Construction Website (WebAward)
  • "A Refined Build Experience" as positioning
  • Judged on: design, ease of use, copywriting, interactivity, technology, innovation, content

MATT Construction

  • Website showcases commercial general contracting in California
  • Detailed project portfolio, collaboration with architects highlighted
  • Awards and recognitions featured prominently

PCL Construction

  • Full-width project photography
  • User-friendly navigation
  • Safety, quality, innovation messaging baked into the visual experience

Common Mistakes to Flag for Clients

Mistake Why It's Bad What to Do Instead
Generic blue + orange palette Looks like every other contractor Pick ONE bold color and own it. Pair with smart neutrals.
Stock photography Screams "we don't actually do good work" Invest in real project photography. Even iPhone shots > stock.
Clip art or icon-based logos Looks cheap, forgettable Custom wordmark or minimal logomark. Less is more.
No visual system for social Every post looks different, no brand recognition Build templates. Lock colors, fonts, and layout patterns.
Trying to appeal to everyone Results in a brand that connects with no one Define your client: residential homeowner vs commercial PM vs developer. Design for them.
DIY Canva templates Generic by definition since thousands use the same layout Custom design or at minimum heavily customized templates with unique brand elements
Ignoring dark mode / digital Brand only works on white paper Test your palette on dark backgrounds, mobile screens, social feeds
Too cold / too corporate Residential clients want to trust a human, not a corporation Add warmth through photography style, one accent color, or real faces

Color Trends in Construction Branding

What's Overused

  • Navy blue (#003366 range) + safety orange (#FF6600 range)
  • Royal blue + white
  • Red + black (aggressive, dated)
  • Green only when "eco" is the positioning

What's Working

  • Deep, distinctive blues that aren't generic navy (Skanska, Turner, Brasfield & Gorrie all have THEIR blue)
  • Black-forward palettes with one strong accent (modern, premium feel)
  • Warm neutrals (sand, clay, warm gray) for residential/design-build
  • Bold yellow or gold for industrial/heavy construction (Kiewit)
  • Desaturated earth tones for companies leaning into craftsmanship

Emerging

  • Dark backgrounds with light type (premium, editorial feel)
  • Monochromatic palettes with one pop color
  • Muted, filmic color grading on photography (less saturated, more mood)

Typography Patterns

What Dominates

  • Heavy sans-serif wordmarks (Arial Black, Helvetica Bold, custom grotesks)
  • All-caps for logos, mixed case for body
  • Tight letter-spacing on headlines

What's Emerging as Premium

  • Geometric sans-serifs (cleaner than grotesks, more personality than Helvetica)
  • Serif + sans-serif pairings for companies targeting architects/designers
  • Variable weight fonts for flexible systems

Construction-Specific Fonts Worth Noting

  • Zone 33 -- Bridges corporate professionalism and industrial character
  • Abelon -- Bold sans-serif display, merges contemporary + industrial
  • Modified Helvetica remains the backbone of half the industry

Social Media Visual Identity Patterns

The Stats

  • 84% of construction companies are on Instagram
  • But most post inconsistently with no visual system
  • The companies winning on social treat their feed like a portfolio

What Separates Good From Great on Instagram

Good: Consistent posting, decent project photos, branded colors on graphics Great: Every post could stand alone as a portfolio piece. The grid tells a story. Real humans show up alongside the work.

Content Types That Build Brand

  1. Project photography (the backbone)
  2. Behind-the-scenes / process shots (humanizes the brand)
  3. Educational content (positions as thought leader, hardest to create, highest long-term value)
  4. Team / crew content (trust signal, especially as AI content rises)
  5. Before/after transformations (immediate visual impact)

What to Avoid on Social

  • Random job site photos with no composition
  • Overly designed graphics that feel like ads
  • Inconsistent filters or editing styles
  • Stock photography mixed with real photography (kills trust instantly)

Key Takeaway for AOM's Construction Vertical

The opportunity is massive because the bar is so low. Most construction companies in the $1M-$20M range have:

  • A logo from 2008
  • No brand guidelines
  • Stock photos on their website
  • Zero visual consistency on social media

AOM can walk into a pitch with a side-by-side: "This is your Instagram vs this is what NS Builders looks like with 400K followers." The gap sells the service.

The play is:

  1. Steffen builds brand guidelines for each construction client
  2. Tony executes social with those guidelines locked in
  3. Bobby builds web with those guidelines locked in
  4. Every touchpoint looks like the same company

That's the AOM system. That's what $3k/month buys.
